questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Second Derivative of a Parametric Curve
questions.problem: A curve is defined by the parametric equations $x={t}^{3}-1,\,y=3{t}^{6}+2$ where $t$ is a real number. Calculate $\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}.$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the first derivative, we will use the formula

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}.
$$

Differentiating $x$ and $y,$ we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=3{t}^{2},\,{y}^{′}(t)=18{t}^{5}.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{18{t}^{5}}{3{t}^{2}}=6{t}^{3}.
$$

To compute the second derivative, we can use the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{dt}(\frac{dy}{dx})}{(\frac{dx}{dt})}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting into the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{dt}(6{t}^{3})}{3{t}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{18{t}^{2}}{3{t}^{2}} \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: A curve is defined by the parametric equations $x=-2\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)-10,\,y=6\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)+15.$ Calculate $\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}.$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the first derivative, we will use the formula

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}.
$$

Differentiating $x$ and $y,$ we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=8\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t),\,{y}^{′}(t)=24\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t).
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{24\operatorname{cos}⁡(4t)}{8\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)}=3\operatorname{cot}⁡(4t).
$$

To compute the second derivative, we can use the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{dt}(\frac{dy}{dx})}{(\frac{dx}{dt})}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting into the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{dt}(3\operatorname{cot}⁡(4t))}{8\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)} \\  & =-\frac{12{csc}^{2}⁡(4t)}{8\operatorname{sin}⁡(4t)} \\  & =-\frac{3}{2}{csc}^{3}⁡(4t).\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: A curve is defined by the parametric equations $x=3{e}^{5t+1},\,y=5{e}^{2t}-7$ where $t$ is a real number. Calculate $\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}.$
questions.worked_solution:
To find the first derivative, we will use the formula

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}.
$$

Differentiating $x$ and $y,$ we get

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=15{e}^{1+5t},\,{y}^{′}(t)=10{e}^{2t}.
$$

 

Therefore,

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{10{e}^{2t}}{15{e}^{1+5t}}=\frac{2}{3}{e}^{-1-3t}.
$$

To compute the second derivative, we can use the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{dt}(\frac{dy}{dx})}{(\frac{dx}{dt})}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting into the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{dt}(\frac{2}{3}{e}^{-1-3t})}{15{e}^{1+5t}} \\  & =\frac{-2{e}^{-1-3t}}{15{e}^{1+5t}} \\  & =-\frac{2}{15}{e}^{-2-8t}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Derivative of a Parametric Curve at a Given Point
questions.worked_solution:
To compute $\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}},$ we can use the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{dt}(\frac{dy}{dx})}{(\frac{dx}{dt})}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're given that $\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{3}{2}t,$ and we can calculate $\frac{dx}{dt}$ as follows:

$$
\frac{dx}{dt}=\frac{d}{dt}({t}^{2}+1)=2t
$$

Substituting into the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{dt}(\frac{3}{2}t)}{2t} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{3}{2})}{2t} \\  & =\frac{3}{4t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate at $t=2,$ and we get

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}\,{|}_{t\,=\,2}=\frac{3}{4(2)}=\frac{3}{8}.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating the Derivative of a Parametric Curve at a Given Point
questions.worked_solution:
To compute $\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}},$ we can use the formula

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{dt}(\frac{dy}{dx})}{(\frac{dx}{dt})}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're given that $\frac{dy}{dx}=7t+2,$ and we can calculate $\frac{dx}{dt}$ as follows:

$$
\frac{dx}{dt}=\frac{d}{dt}({t}^{5}+1)=5{t}^{4}
$$

Substituting into the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}} & =\frac{\frac{d}{dt}(7t+2)}{5{t}^{4}} \\  & =\frac{(7)}{5{t}^{4}} \\  & =\frac{7}{5{t}^{4}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate at $t=2,$ and we get

$$
\frac{{\text{d}}^{2}y}{\text{d}{x}^{2}}\,{|}_{t\,=\,2}=\frac{7}{5({2}^{4})}=\frac{7}{80}.
$$
